# Matrix calculus for backpropagation {#sec-matrix-calculus}

This appendix collects the backward rules used by GlassNN, in the notation
of @sec-autodiff. $L$ is a scalar (the loss); for every array $z$ the
*adjoint* $\bar z = \partial L / \partial z$ has the shape of $z$. A
backward rule maps the adjoint of an output to the adjoints of the inputs:
it is a vector-Jacobian product, and it never forms the Jacobian
[@griewank2008evaluating; @baydin2018automatic]. When an array is used
several times, its adjoints are added.

The rules are derived by writing the change of $L$,
$\delta L = \langle \bar z, \delta z \rangle$ (the sum of elementwise
products), and expressing $\delta z$ through $\delta a$: the factor that
multiplies $\delta a$ is $\bar a$ [@goodfellow2016deep, chapter 6].

## Shapes: sums, broadcasting, reshaping

| Forward | Backward |
|---|---|
| $z = \sum_j a_{ij}$ | $\bar a_{ij} = \bar z_i$ (copy along the summed axis) |
| $z = \frac1n \sum_j a_{ij}$ | $\bar a_{ij} = \bar z_i / n$ |
| $z = a + b$, $b$ broadcast along an axis | $\bar a = \bar z$, $\bar b = \sum_\text{axis} \bar z$ |
| $z = \operatorname{reshape}(a)$, $z = a^\top$, $z = \operatorname{permute}(a)$ | $\bar a = $ the inverse reshape, transpose or permutation of $\bar z$ |
| $z = a[\text{index}]$ | $\bar a = 0$, then $\bar a[\text{index}] \mathrel{+}= \bar z$ (repeated indices add up) |

Broadcasting copies an array along an axis, so its adjoint *sums* over that
axis: this is `_unbroadcast` in `glassnn.tensor`. Indexing with repeated
indices uses `add.at`, which adds instead of overwriting.

## Elementwise operations

| Forward | Backward |
|---|---|
| $z = f(a)$ | $\bar a = \bar z \odot f'(a)$ |
| $z = a \odot b$ | $\bar a = \bar z \odot b$, $\bar b = \bar z \odot a$ |
| $z = a / b$ | $\bar a = \bar z / b$, $\bar b = -\bar z \odot a / b^2$ |
| $z = a^p$ | $\bar a = \bar z \odot p\, a^{p-1}$ |
| $z = \max(a, 0)$ | $\bar a = \bar z \odot [a > 0]$ |
| $z = \sigma(a)$ | $\bar a = \bar z \odot z \odot (1 - z)$ |
| $z = \tanh a$ | $\bar a = \bar z \odot (1 - z^2)$ |

The derivative is often cheapest in terms of the *output* $z$, which the
forward pass keeps.

## Matrix products and linear layers

For $Z = AB$ with $A \in \R^{m \times k}$ and $B \in \R^{k \times n}$,
$\delta L = \langle \bar Z, \delta A\, B + A\, \delta B \rangle$ gives

$$
\bar A = \bar Z B^\top, \qquad \bar B = A^\top \bar Z .
$$ {#eq-app-matmul}

Each adjoint has the shape of its input, which is a useful check. For a
linear layer on a batch, $Y = X W^\top + \mathbf 1 b^\top$ with
$X \in \R^{N \times n}$, $W \in \R^{m \times n}$:

$$
\bar X = \bar Y W, \qquad \bar W = \bar Y^\top X, \qquad
\bar b = \sum_{i=1}^N \bar Y_{i,:} .
$$ {#eq-app-linear}

The bias is broadcast over the batch, so its adjoint sums over it.

## Softmax, log-softmax and cross-entropy

For one row, $s = \operatorname{softmax}(a)$ has Jacobian
$\operatorname{diag}(s) - s s^\top$, hence

$$
\bar a = s \odot \bigl(\bar s - \langle \bar s, s \rangle\bigr).
$$

For $z = \log \operatorname{softmax}(a)$, $\bar a = \bar z - s \sum_k \bar z_k$.
The cross-entropy of a row with true class $y$,
$\ell = -\log s_y$, combines the two into

$$
\bar a = \bar \ell\, (s - e_y),
$$ {#eq-app-ce}

with $e_y$ the one-hot vector of $y$; averaging over a batch of $N$ rows
divides by $N$. With label smoothing $\varepsilon$, $e_y$ is replaced by
$(1 - \varepsilon) e_y + \varepsilon / C$.

## Normalization

With $\hat x = (x - \mu) / \sqrt{\sigma^2 + \varepsilon}$, the mean $\mu$
and the biased variance $\sigma^2$ taken over $m$ elements (a row for
layer normalization, a feature over the batch for batch normalization),

$$
\bar x = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\sigma^2 + \varepsilon}} \Bigl(\bar{\hat x}
- \operatorname{mean}(\bar{\hat x})
- \hat x \operatorname{mean}(\bar{\hat x} \odot \hat x)\Bigr).
$$

The two subtracted terms account for $\mu$ and $\sigma$ depending on $x$.

## Convolution and pooling

Im2col rewrites a convolution as a matrix product [@chellapilla2006high]:
the windows of the input become the columns of a matrix $U$, the filters
the rows of $W_\text{mat}$, and $Y = W_\text{mat} U$. By
@eq-app-matmul, $\bar W_\text{mat} = \bar Y U^\top$ and
$\bar U = W_\text{mat}^\top \bar Y$; since windows overlap, an input element
appears in several columns of $U$ and its adjoint is the *sum* of the
corresponding entries of $\bar U$ ("col2im"). Max pooling passes the adjoint
to the position of the maximum of each window; average pooling spreads it
evenly over the window.

## Attention

For $S = Q K^\top / \sqrt d$, $A = \operatorname{softmax}(S)$ row by row,
and $Z = A V$ (@sec-attention):

$$
\bar V = A^\top \bar Z, \quad \bar A = \bar Z V^\top, \quad
\bar S = A \odot \bigl(\bar A - \operatorname{rowsum}(\bar A \odot A)\bigr), \quad
\bar Q = \frac{\bar S K}{\sqrt d}, \quad \bar K = \frac{\bar S^\top Q}{\sqrt d}.
$$

A mask adds $-\infty$ to some scores; the corresponding weights are 0 and
receive no gradient.

## Check a rule numerically

Every rule above is tested in GlassNN against central finite differences
with `{python} api_link("glassnn.gradcheck.gradcheck")`. The same check
confirms @eq-app-linear for a hand-written layer:

```{python}
import numpy as np

from glassnn import Tensor
from glassnn.gradcheck import gradcheck

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X, W, b = (
    Tensor(rng.normal(size=shape), requires_grad=True, dtype="float64")
    for shape in [(4, 3), (2, 3), (2,)]
)
print(gradcheck(lambda X, W, b: X @ W.T + b, [X, W, b]))

Y_bar = np.cos(np.arange(1, 9)).reshape(4, 2)  # the weights gradcheck uses
print(np.allclose(W.grad.data, Y_bar.T @ X.data))  # W-bar = Y-bar^T X
```
